results.title: What is a Milestone Schedule? Definition and Example
results.content: A milestone schedule is a tool that aids project managers in achieving this goal so that the project can be completed on time and within budget. > **Definition:** A **milestone schedule**or**milestone chart** is a timeline that uses milestones to divide project work into phases for easy monitoring. Project managers split project work into portions as milestones for simple tracking since tracking a large project with a milestone schedule is difficult. A work breakdown structure breaks the project work into milestones as shown below: The milestone schedule is an output of the planning process. An Example of a Milestone Schedule Each deliverable at the milestone is assessed with different color codes as RGA (Red/Green/Amber): * **Green** indicates that the team has fully met the criteria for the deliverable * **Amber/Yellow** indicates that the criteria have not been fully met, but the team has a work plan to achieve the criteria * **Red** indicates that the team has not fully met the criteria and has no plan to meet the criteria (requiring help from management) The milestone is approved if the metrics for all deliverables are green. The project manager’s first scheduling responsibility is to define project objectives by putting them into quantitative terms. You must logically categorize the work to generate milestones once the project objectives have been defined. Once defined, the project manager should ensure that the milestones are realistic. The project manager must also ensure that the milestones are sensibly ordered and organized. ### Milestone Schedule Vs Master Schedule A project master schedule is a tool for early communication among stakeholders that displays major deliverables, milestones, and a summary of the work breakdown structure. During this stage, the project manager establishes the framework for management control, defines the project objectives, identifies the activities required to complete the project, and estimates the resources and time required to complete the project. The project milestone schedule is an important planning and control tool for project managers. results.title: Deliverables Acceptance Management – Setting Criteria for Accepting Project Deliverables
results.content: # Deliverables Acceptance Management – Setting Criteria for Accepting Project Deliverables. **Deliverables acceptance management** starts when the project manager develops a project plan and subordinated plans through communicating with the customer, team and other stakeholders. It is a coherent process that takes a number of stages and ends up with setting up criteria for reviewing results and accepting deliverables of a project. This person can play the ***role of approver*** who evaluates the deliverables at the project’s end, communicates with the customer on this point, and make the final decision on accepting and approving the deliverables. Sometimes, a delegate of the quality control & assurance team takes the role of approver and in collaboration with the project manager this person develops the criteria for accepting project deliverables. Also a representative of the customer is involved in setting deliverables acceptance criteria and reviewing project results. Reviewer works closely with the project team and the project manager on the point of setting deliverables acceptance criteria. **Deliverables acceptance management** requires the project manager to take care of the project’s feasibility and make sure it is done in line with the Business Case and customer expectations. The ultimate goal of **deliverables acceptance management** is to ensure successful delivery of expected project results in a specified time period, within budget and within scope. * Set up the criteria for accepting project deliverables, coming to agreement with the customer. * Determine and assign a person who will review the deliverables and assure their adherence to the criteria listed in the project acceptance plan (as it’s been said, normally the project manager accomplishes this task but there can be exceptions). * Set up any time considerations that may be required for managing the acceptance of project deliverables and adherence to customer expectations. **Deliverables acceptance management** is a complicated and highly important process that determines success of a project in terms of deliverables produced. Every project manager must take care of doing a series of tasks for reviewing and accepting project deliverables. The process of managing project deliverables involves the role of reviewer and the role of approver.

results.title: 6.6  Deliverables Acceptance Plan - PM2 Agile Projects
results.content: # 6.6 Deliverables Acceptance Plan. # 6.6  Deliverables Acceptance Plan. Deliverables acceptance planning aims to **increase the likelihood that deliverables will be accepted by the client side** and that the resources involved in the acceptance will be used in an efficient way. The Deliverables Acceptance Plan documents the agreed **criteria** and **approach** for deliverables acceptance. It also documents the relevant **responsibilities**, including all activities and **effort required**, as well as the **timing** and **capability requirements** for this so that the project’s deliverable(s) can be formally accepted by the client based on **objective criteria and predefined timelines**. Align the deliverables acceptance process with the requirements validation activities as well as with other testing and quality control activities. * Ensure that all project deliverables are accounted for **including any support material** (user manuals, etc.). * Note that deliverables acceptance activities **may not happen (only) at the end of the Executing Phase**, but can follow the project’s delivery schedule. * Include the **deliverables acceptance activities** (and **resources** required) in the Project Work Plan. * The guidelines set out in the **Deliverables Acceptance Plan template** can be used to help tailor a deliverables acceptance process for any given project. 2. Define the **acceptance criteria** and **tolerances** for the project deliverables and define the **activities needed** to achieve their validation. 3. Define the **process** and **timeline** for **dealing with non-acceptance (or partial acceptance)**. 4. Define the **level of formality** of the acceptance process (e.g. whether a signed Deliverables Acceptance Note is required, etc.). 5. Define clear roles and **responsibilities** for the acceptance of each deliverable:. * Determine who is responsible for the activities leading up to the acceptance of the **deliverable**. * Identify the **stakeholders** who will **validate** the deliverable and define the specific knowledge and skills they require. * Identify the **person/group responsible for the final acceptance** of the deliverable. 6. **Tailor the Deliverables Acceptance Checklist** based on the acceptance activities defined. 7. In the case of outsourced work, the Deliverable Acceptance Process should be **documented in the contract**. 8. Ensure that the Deliverables Acceptance Plan is **communicated** to the relevant project stakeholders. * Deliverables Acceptance Plan (PM2 Template). * Deliverables Acceptance Checklist (setup)(PM2 Template). 6.6 Deliverables Acceptance Plan.

results.title: Criteria for Accepting Deliverables – Bonnie Biafore
results.content: You are here: Home / Project Management / Criteria for Accepting Deliverables. # Criteria for Accepting Deliverables. What criteria do you use to accept a deliverable? Here are criteria for deciding whether to accept a deliverable and close project tasks. * **Deliverables have been produced and can be reviewed.** You can’t accept a deliverable if it doesn’t exist yet – or you don’t know that it’s ready. * **Acceptance criteria are met.** The next level criteria is that the deliverable passes the tests and meets the stakeholders expectations. (This is why it’s important to document acceptance criteria before work starts on tasks.) If stakeholders aren’t satisfied, a task needs to stay open or new tasks have to be added to your schedule to correct the deliverable, so it meets expectations. In some cases, deliverables need to be reviewed by other stakeholders after acceptance criteria are met, for example, customer reviews. Sometimes deeper examination is called for before accepting a deliverable and closing project tasks. If you find scope creep in a product, you should consider whether to accept a deliverable or ask your team member to remove the scope creep item and re-submit their product for review and task closure. For example, you might not accept the deliverable with scope creep until it has passed the change control process. * **Complete a detailed quality audit.** At times, particularly in regulated industries, products aren’t considered viable until certified personnel have conducted a detailed review or audit, (medical instruments for example.) This activity usually goes above and beyond the acceptance criteria provided by internal stakeholders. * **Does the deliverable include appropriate documentation?** If you don’t have a separate project task for creating product documentation, documentation needs to be delivered along with its corresponding deliverables before accepting the deliverable and closing the task. * **Does the deliverables support successor tasks sufficiently?** This acceptance criteria is often missing: whether the deliverable provides what successor tasks need. In this case, consider whether to accept the deliverable. results.title: How to Define Project Deliverables and Acceptance Criteria
results.content: # How can you define project deliverables and acceptance criteria for Operational Planning? How to define project deliverables and acceptance criteria? Why are project deliverables and acceptance criteria important? One of the key aspects of operational planning is to define the project deliverables and acceptance criteria, which are the outputs and standards that the project must produce and meet to satisfy the stakeholders and customers. In this article, you will learn how to define project deliverables and acceptance criteria for operational planning, and why they are important for project success. ## 1 What are project deliverables? Project deliverables should be clearly defined in terms of their features, functions, quality, and specifications, and they should align with the project objectives and the stakeholder expectations. Acceptance criteria are the measurable and verifiable conditions that the project deliverables must meet to be accepted by the stakeholders and customers. Acceptance criteria should be defined before the project starts, and they should be realistic, achievable, and agreed upon by all parties involved. ## 3 How to define project deliverables and acceptance criteria? Defining project deliverables and acceptance criteria for operational planning can be made easier with the use of several steps and tools. Lastly, a requirements traceability matrix (RTM) links project requirements to deliverables and acceptance criteria so that they are traceable and verifiable throughout the lifecycle. All of these tools can help to ensure that deliverables and acceptance criteria are aligned with project requirements. ## 4 Why are project deliverables and acceptance criteria important? Defining project deliverables and acceptance criteria for operational planning is important for a variety of reasons. These include providing a clear and common understanding of what the project must produce and how it will be evaluated, managing the project scope to avoid scope creep, monitoring and controlling the project progress and performance, ensuring quality and customer satisfaction, and facilitating the project closure and acceptance. By defining deliverables and acceptance criteria, you can ensure that your project runs smoothly and meets the needs of stakeholders and customers.
